claims.claim: Treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin mimicked the downregulation of p-S6 in the right GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice and also in both hindlimbs of WT pups.
claims.source: We further found that this downregulation could be mimicked in the right GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice and also in both hindlimbs of WT pups by treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin, which also stunts overall growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and bone length measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E.

claims.claim: FGF signaling was not increased in any region of the left GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P3.
claims.source: Since FGFs secreted by the perichondrium negatively regulate chondrocyte proliferation and early hypertrophy (Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016), we tested whether FGF signaling was altered, but did not detect an increase in FGF signaling in any region of the left GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–B').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–B', and citations to Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Fgfr3 expression was downregulated in the region of the left GP where the secondary ossification center forms in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: On the contrary, Fgfr3 expression was downregulated in the region of the left GP where the secondary ossification center forms, suggesting Fgfr3 could be involved in the observed delayed formation and expansion of this structure.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data (referenced in the context of Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–B').

claims.claim: MCP5 mRNA or protein was not detected in P1-Pit::DTR mice at P3.
claims.source: Moreover, decreased TGFβR2 signaling in the joint region has been shown to impair chondrocyte hypertrophy at embryonic stages via increased expression of the cytokine MCP5 (Longobardi et al., 2012), but we were not able to detect MCP5 mRNA or protein in our model at P3.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of detection of MCP5 in the experimental model, and cites Longobardi et al., 2012.

claims.claim: RNA and protein levels of the WNT target Lef1 were upregulated in the RZ of the left P1-Pit::DTR GP compared to right.
claims.source: On the other hand, RNA and protein levels of the WNT target Lef1 were upregulated in the RZ of the left P1-Pit::DTR GP compared to right (Figure 3C; see also Figure 4—figure supplement 2, n = 5 at P3, 4 at P4, 3 at P5), which might impair PTHLH signaling and chondrocyte differentiation, as described (Ray et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and citations to Ray et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Igf1 was highly expressed in the right infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) but was extremely and specifically downregulated in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at 2-3dpi.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that while Igf1 was highly expressed in the right infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP), an extra-synovial adipose tissue located between the femur and the tibia, it was extremely and specifically downregulated in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at 2-3dpi (Figure 4A, n = 10/12), and recovered by 4dpi (Figure 4A', n = 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A and 4A'.

claims.claim: Igf1 expression recovered in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice by 4dpi.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that while Igf1 was highly expressed in the right infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP), an extra-synovial adipose tissue located between the femur and the tibia, it was extremely and specifically downregulated in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at 2-3dpi (Figure 4A, n = 10/12), and recovered by 4dpi (Figure 4A', n = 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A'.

claims.claim: Igf1 expression was not consistently altered in other tissues, such as the perichondrium, the muscle bundles or cells in the metaphyseal region.
claims.source: Furthermore, Igf1 expression was not consistently altered in other tissues, such as the perichondrium, the muscle bundles or cells in the metaphyseal (shaft) region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Only minor to no changes were detected in the expression of Igf2 or the main IGF receptor gene Igf1r in the GP or surrounding tissues.
claims.source: Similarly, we only detected minor to no changes in the expression of Igf2 or the main IGF receptor gene Igf1r in the GP or surrounding tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C), indicating that the IPFP was specifically affected by the insult.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claims.claim: Differential expression of SOCS3 between the left and right GPs was not detected at P2 or P3 in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: In particular, since injury-induced inflammation (see below) could conceivably increase expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 (SOCS3), which is known to exert a negative influence on IGF signaling (Ahmed and Farquharson, 2010), we performed SOCS3 immunohistochemistry on P1-Pit::DTR knee sections. However, we could not detect differential expression between the left and right GPs at P2 or P3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that it is the reduced availability of IGF1 from the IPFP that causes some of the signaling changes observed in the left GP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, and citation to Ahmed and Farquharson, 2010.

claims.claim: Exogenous IGF1 provided by intraarticular injections in P1-Pit::DTR pups (P1-P3) consistently rescued mTORC1 signaling in the PZ and pre-HZ of the GPs.
claims.source: To test this possibility, we provided exogenous IGF1 to the left knee region by intraarticular injections in P1-Pit::DTR pups (P1-P3), and found that indeed mTORC1 signaling was consistently rescued in the PZ and pre-HZ of the GPs (Figure 4B' top, n = 5 P3-P5 pups).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B'.

claims.claim: Ihh and Fgfr3 expression were rescued in IGF1-injected P1-Pit::DTR animals.
claims.source: Curiously, Ihh and Fgfr3 expression were also rescued in these animals (Figure 4B' bottom, n = 3 at P3, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that both genes are downstream of IGF signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Left-specific neutrophil recruitment was observed in the IPFP at P2-P4 in P1-Pit::DTR mice and had mostly receded by P5.
claims.source: We observed left-specific neutrophil recruitment at P2-P4 that had mostly receded by P5, thus precisely correlating with transient Igf1 downregulation (Figure 4C–C' n = 5, 5, 4, 5 at P2, P3, P4, P5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C–C'.

claims.claim: Macrophages were additionally recruited to the left IPFP in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: Moreover, macrophages, already very abundant in the IPFP in resting conditions, were additionally recruited to the left IPFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–A').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–A'.

claims.claim: Neutrophil blockade with the NIMP-R14 neutralizing antibody significantly correlated with partial recovery of Igf1 expression in the IPFP.
claims.source: As neutrophils are an important feature of joint inflammatory diseases (Wright et al., 2010; Wipke and Allen, 2001), we tested whether neutrophils were responsible for Igf1 downregulation by blocking their recruitment with the NIMP-R14 neutralizing antibody (Lopez et al., 1984) during P1-P3 in P1-Pit::DTR mice. Neutrophil blockade was effective for at least 14 hr (Figure 4D, n = 3), and significantly correlated with partial recovery of Igf1 expression in the IPFP (Figure 4D', n = 4), without inhibiting cell death in this region (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D', and citations to Wright et al., 2010; Wipke and Allen, 2001; Lopez et al., 1984.

claims.claim: The recovery of Igf1 expression after neutrophil blockade correlated with increased levels of p-S6 and Ihh in the pre-HZ.
claims.source: Importantly, the recovery of Igf1 expression correlated with increased levels of p-S6 and Ihh in the pre-HZ (Figure 4D'', n = 3, and not shown), demonstrating that proper signaling in the pre-HZ requires IGF1 production from the IPFP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D''.

claims.claim: LPS injection into the joint of WT animals caused a strong local recruitment of neutrophils to the IPFP and led to downregulation of Igf1 in the areas with highest accumulation of neutrophils.
claims.source: To further probe the role of immune-cell recruitment in Igf1 downregulation, we injected lipopolysaccharide (LPS) into the joint of WT animals, which caused a strong (but patchy) local recruitment of neutrophils to the IPFP. Of significance, this recruitment led to the predicted downregulation of Igf1 in the areas with highest accumulation of neutrophils (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: LPS-induced neutrophil recruitment led to Igf1 downregulation in the absence of cell death.
claims.source: This effect took place in the absence of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), suggesting that immune cells (probably neutrophils) secrete factors that reduce Igf1 expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: TNFα-expressing cells (some of them neutrophils) were present in the left and not the right IPFP in P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2.
claims.source: Notably, we found that TNFα-expressing cells (some of them neutrophils) were present in the left and not the right IPFP in P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2, and that neutrophils accumulated TNFα in what seemed to be the Golgi apparatus (Figure 4C''').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C'''.

claims.claim: TNFα has been shown to reduce Igf1 expression in vascular smooth muscle.
claims.source: TNFα has been shown to reduce Igf1 expression in vascular smooth muscle (Anwar et al., 2002), raising the possibility that this cytokine is in part responsible for the observed Igf1 downregulation in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Anwar et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Partial restoration of Igf1 expression by neutrophil blockade did not rescue Fgfr3 expression.
claims.source: Interestingly, partial restoration of Igf1 expression by neutrophil blockade did not rescue Fgfr3 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that full restoration of Igf1 is necessary for normal Fgfr3 expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Neither IGF1 injection nor neutrophil blockade were sufficient to rescue the decreased left bone growth at P4.
claims.source: Despite IGF1 supplementation rescuing several critical pathways, neither IGF1 injection nor neutrophil blockade were sufficient to rescue the decreased left bone growth at P4 (Figure 4E–F, n = 5 experimental and 5 control animals for each treatment), indicating that an IGF1-independent pathway also contributes to the growth defect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 4E–F.

claims.claim: Expression of Lef1 in the left GP remained upregulated after IGF1 injection or neutrophil blockade.
claims.source: Indeed, expression of Lef1 in the left GP remained upregulated after IGF1 injection or neutrophil blockade (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B), raising the possibility that increased LEF1 activity contributes to the growth defect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B.

claims.claim: Expression of Early growth response gene 1 (Egr1) was increased in the left IPFP and pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2 (1dpi).
claims.source: Given the importance of the immediate-early damage response upon injury, we tested its activation and indeed detected it in the left joint region of P1-Pit::DTR mice, not only in the IPFP but also in the prospective articular cartilage (pAC). Specifically, we observed that expression of Early growth response gene 1 (Egr1) was increased in the left IPFP and pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2 (1dpi) (Figure 5A, n = 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Egr1 expression in the left IPFP receded by P3, but remained highly upregulated in the left pAC through P4, receding by P5.
claims.source: Egr1 expression in the left IPFP receded by P3, but remained highly upregulated in the left pAC through P4, receding by P5 (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B, n = 3, 2, 2, respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: p-S6 expression was upregulated in the left pAC at P3 and P4 and receded by P5.
claims.source: Interestingly, p-S6 expression, while downregulated in the pre-HZ (Figures 3 and 4), was upregulated in the left pAC at P3 and P4 and receded by P5 (Figure 5B–C, n = 33, 14 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B', n = 2), suggesting transiently increased mTORC1 signaling in this region, as observed in osteoarthritis (Pal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B', and citation to Pal et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of Hif2a was detected in the left pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: For example, we detected ectopic expression of Hif2a (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which has a prominent role in cartilage destruction during osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis (Ryu et al., 2014; Husa et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Ryu et al., 2014; Husa et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Il6 was upregulated in the left pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: In addition, Il6, one of the main mediators of Hif2a-dependent cartilage destruction (Ryu et al., 2014), was upregulated in the left pAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and was the likely cause of the ectopic JAK1/2-dependent expression of p-STAT3 we detected in the pAC at P3 and P4 (Figure 5B–C, n = 13 and 3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and that receded by P5 (not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Ryu et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Ectopic JAK1/2-dependent expression of p-STAT3 was detected in the pAC at P3 and P4 in P1-Pit::DTR mice and receded by P5.
claims.source: In addition, Il6, one of the main mediators of Hif2a-dependent cartilage destruction (Ryu et al., 2014), was upregulated in the left pAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and was the likely cause of the ectopic JAK1/2-dependent expression of p-STAT3 we detected in the pAC at P3 and P4 (Figure 5B–C, n = 13 and 3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and that receded by P5 (not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Expression of Egr1, p-S6 and p-STAT3 in the pAC was not due to inflammation in the IPFP, as neutrophil blockade or injection of IGF1 did not preclude activation of the injury response in the pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: Importantly, expression of Egr1, p-S6 and p-STAT3 was not due to inflammation in the IPFP, as neutrophil blockade or injection of IGF1 did not preclude activation of the injury response in the pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Histological analysis revealed extensive and persistent cell loss in the pAC/AC from P4 to at least P27.
claims.source: Associated with the injury response, histological analysis revealed extensive and persistent cell loss in the pAC/AC from P4 to at least P27 (Figure 5D–E, n = 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5D–E.

claims.claim: Most signaling changes in the pAC extended beyond the area of cell death, almost reaching into the RZ of the GP.
claims.source: Of note, most signaling changes extended beyond the area of cell death (i.e. the pAC), almost reaching into the RZ of the GP (compare TUNEL and p-STAT3 in Figure 5B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of TUNEL and p-STAT3 staining in Figure 5B–C.

claims.claim: Cells in the pAC/AC do not normally give rise to GP chondrocytes.
claims.source: Since cells in the pAC/AC do not normally give rise to GP chondrocytes (Kozhemyakina et al., 2015), this set of results raised the possibility that the injury response in the pAC triggers a paracrine-signaling cascade that contributes to the signaling defects observed in the RZ.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kozhemyakina et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In vivo treatment with the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib precluded p-STAT3 and LEF1 upregulation in the articular region of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: Significantly, in vivo treatment with the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib (Fridman et al., 2010) precluded p-STAT3 and LEF1 upregulation in the articular region of P1-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–A').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–A', and citation to Fridman et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Ruxolitinib failed to rescue bone growth in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: However, like IGF1 injection, ruxolitinib failed to rescue bone growth (Figure 6A–B, n = 5), perhaps because mTORC1 signaling remained downregulated in the pre-HZ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 6A–B and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C'.

claims.claim: The combined treatment of ruxolitinib and intraarticular IGF1 had a significant rescue effect on bone growth in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: Finally, we tested whether redundancies exist between the fat pad-HZ axis and the pAC-RZ axis by administering ruxolitinib and intraarticular IGF1 either individually or in combination in the same litters. Notably, unlike single treatments, the combined treatment had a significant rescue effect (Figure 6A–B), although only some femora (3 out of 11) and none of the tibiae showed complete rescue (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claims.claim: Only some femora (3 out of 11) and none of the tibiae showed complete rescue after combined treatment with ruxolitinib and IGF1.
claims.source: Finally, we tested whether redundancies exist between the fat pad-HZ axis and the pAC-RZ axis by administering ruxolitinib and intraarticular IGF1 either individually or in combination in the same litters. Notably, unlike single treatments, the combined treatment had a significant rescue effect (Figure 6A–B), although only some femora (3 out of 11) and none of the tibiae showed complete rescue (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claims.claim: Analysis of cell death 3-4dpi in P14-Pit::DTR mice revealed apoptotic cells only in the surrounding soft tissues, and not the GP.
claims.source: Similar to the P1 injections, analysis of cell death 3-4dpi in P14-Pit::DTR mice revealed apoptotic cells only in the surrounding soft tissues, and not the GP (Figure 7A, n = 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The height of the left HZ zone at 4dpi was reduced in P14-Pit::DTR mice compared to controls.
claims.source: As in the P1-Pit::DTR model, the height of the left HZ zone at 4dpi was reduced in P14-Pit::DTR mice compared to controls (Figure 7B, n = 2), and the hindlimbs developed a progressive left-right asymmetry over time, although it was non-significant at P20 (~7–13% by P57, Figure 7F–G, n = 3–4 per genotype at P20, n = 7 per genotype at P57).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The hindlimbs of P14-Pit::DTR mice developed a progressive left-right asymmetry over time, although it was non-significant at P20 (~7–13% by P57).
claims.source: As in the P1-Pit::DTR model, the height of the left HZ zone at 4dpi was reduced in P14-Pit::DTR mice compared to controls (Figure 7B, n = 2), and the hindlimbs developed a progressive left-right asymmetry over time, although it was non-significant at P20 (~7–13% by P57, Figure 7F–G, n = 3–4 per genotype at P20, n = 7 per genotype at P57).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 7F–G.

claims.claim: Although neutrophils infiltrated the knee joint in P14-Pit::DTR mice, mTORC1 activity and Ihh signaling were not reduced at 3-4dpi in the left HZ as compared to the right.
claims.source: Furthermore, although neutrophils infiltrated the knee joint, mTORC1 activity and Ihh signaling were not reduced at 3-4dpi in the left HZ as compared to the right in P14-Pit::DTR mice, unlike in the P1-Pit::DTR experiment (Figure 7C, n = 4 and not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Igf1 is no longer expressed in the right nor the left IPFP at P17-18.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that Igf1 is no longer expressed in the right nor the left IPFP at P17-18 (Figure 7D, inset, n = 3), suggesting that mTORC1 activity in the HZ eventually becomes independent of this extrinsic source of IGF1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Similar to P1-Pit::DTR mice, Egr1 and LEF1 were ectopically activated in the left cartilage of P14-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: On the other hand, similar to P1-Pit::DTR mice, Egr1 and LEF1 were ectopically activated in the left cartilage of P14-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 7D–E, n = 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7D–E.

claims.claim: The IPFP appeared as a defined region at around E17.5.
claims.source: The IPFP appeared as a defined region at around E17.5, and this coincided with the accumulation of a high level of Igf1 expression in the area as compared to the surrounding mesenchymal tissues.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on histological and in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The appearance of the IPFP at E17.5 coincided with the accumulation of a high level of Igf1 expression in the area as compared to the surrounding mesenchymal tissues.
claims.source: The IPFP appeared as a defined region at around E17.5, and this coincided with the accumulation of a high level of Igf1 expression in the area as compared to the surrounding mesenchymal tissues.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) were detected in the interzone area even before the IPFP was formed.
claims.source: While perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) (Hindle et al., 2017) were detected in the interzone area even before the IPFP was formed, adipocytes (detected either by hematoxylin and eosin staining or expression of FABP4) were not clearly seen until P3-P4, indicating that adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Hindle et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Adipocytes were not clearly seen in the IPFP until P3-P4, indicating that adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
claims.source: While perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) (Hindle et al., 2017) were detected in the interzone area even before the IPFP was formed, adipocytes (detected either by hematoxylin and eosin staining or expression of FABP4) were not clearly seen until P3-P4, indicating that adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on histological and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Igf1 expression levels gradually decreased postnatally until they were barely detectable at P8 and not detected at P12.
claims.source: As expected, Igf1 expression levels gradually decreased postnatally until they were barely detectable at P8 and not detected at P12.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The radius grows more slowly than the tibia at the stages when Igf1 levels are high in the IPFP, whereas the ratio stabilizes after P8, roughly coinciding with the cessation of Igf1 expression.
claims.source: Intrigued by the dynamic expression of Igf1 in the IPFP, we finally explored whether the dynamics correlate with any change in the ratio of the lengths of the radius (far from any fat pad, see Figure 7—figure supplement 1A') and the tibia during development. Interestingly, we observed that the radius grows more slowly than the tibia at the stages when Igf1 levels are high in the IPFP, whereas the ratio stabilizes after P8, roughly coinciding with the cessation of Igf1 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bone length ratio measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Transient cell death in the early postnatal left hindlimb mesenchyme surrounding the GPs leads to reduced long bone growth due to altered signaling from two tissues in the adjacent knee joint.
claims.source: Our study demonstrates that transient cell death in the early postnatal left hindlimb mesenchyme surrounding the GPs leads to reduced long bone growth due to altered signaling from two tissues in the adjacent knee joint.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the entire set of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy in the GP.
claims.source: Only a few recent studies have addressed the regulation of longitudinal bone growth by the surrounding tissues, and showed that TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy in the GP (Longobardi et al., 2012), and FGFs produced by the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth in a GP non-autonomous fashion (Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Longobardi et al., 2012.

claims.claim: FGFs produced by the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth in a GP non-autonomous fashion.
claims.source: Only a few recent studies have addressed the regulation of longitudinal bone growth by the surrounding tissues, and showed that TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy in the GP (Longobardi et al., 2012), and FGFs produced by the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth in a GP non-autonomous fashion (Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The study identifies two neonatal joint components that can modulate bone growth, at least following injury: the IPFP and the pAC/AC.
claims.source: Of significance, our study identifies two neonatal joint components that can modulate bone growth, at least following injury: the IPFP and the pAC/AC.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Extrinsic signals from the IPFP and/or pAC/AC modulate distinct GP-intrinsic signaling pathways, leading to reduced bone growth, even in the absence of intrinsic damage to the GP.
claims.source: Taken together, our data support a model whereby extrinsic signals from the IPFP and/or pAC/AC modulate distinct GP-intrinsic signaling pathways, leading to reduced bone growth, even in the absence of intrinsic damage to the GP (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and model shown in Figure 6C–D.

claims.claim: The apparently milder rescue of the tibia compared to the femur could mean that each bone's response to the same growth-modulating cues varies with the developmental stage in a different manner.
claims.source: While we think this model can be generally applied, the apparently milder rescue of the tibia compared to the femur (Figure 6B) could mean that each bone's response to the same growth-modulating cues varies with the developmental stage in a different manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The specific effect of limb immobilization on the growth of different bones has recently been shown to depend on the time of treatment in chicken and crocodile embryos.
claims.source: Indeed, the specific effect of limb immobilization on the growth of different bones has recently been shown to depend on the time of treatment in chicken and crocodile embryos (Pollard et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pollard et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines can exert a negative influence on bone growth that continues well beyond the cytokine exposure period.
claims.source: This result is reminiscent of in vitro studies showing that pro-inflammatory cytokines can exert a negative influence on bone growth that continues well beyond the cytokine exposure period (MacRae et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to MacRae et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The inflammation-dependent in vitro growth defect was only partially rescued by IGF1 treatment.
claims.source: As in our in vivo study, the inflammation-dependent in vitro growth defect was only partially rescued by IGF1 treatment (Mårtensson et al., 2004), suggesting that inflammation impairs bone growth via both IGF-dependent and -independent pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mårtensson et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-HZ correlates with loss of Ihh expression in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: Using our P1-Pit::DTR mice, we also uncovered that loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-HZ correlates with loss of Ihh expression, and that restoration of IGF1 levels in the joint rescues both pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing correlation between mTORC1 and Ihh signaling.

claims.claim: Restoration of IGF1 levels in the joint rescues both mTORC1 and Ihh signaling pathways.
claims.source: Using our P1-Pit::DTR mice, we also uncovered that loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-HZ correlates with loss of Ihh expression, and that restoration of IGF1 levels in the joint rescues both pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing IGF1 injection rescues mTORC1 and Ihh signaling.

claims.claim: SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity.
claims.source: At the same time, SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity, and mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals (Sanchez et al., 2009), nor does it impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice (Figure 4B'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B'' and citation to Sanchez et al., 2009.

claims.claim: mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals.
claims.source: At the same time, SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity, and mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals (Sanchez et al., 2009), nor does it impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice (Figure 4B'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sanchez et al., 2009.

claims.claim: mTORC1 inhibition does not impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice.
claims.source: At the same time, SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity, and mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals (Sanchez et al., 2009), nor does it impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice (Figure 4B'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B''.

claims.claim: IGF1 activates Ihh expression via an mTORC1-independent pathway, possibly by inhibition of SHP2.
claims.source: Therefore, we speculate that IGF1 activates Ihh expression via an mTORC1-independent pathway, possibly by inhibition of SHP2 (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental data, as indicated by the word 'speculate'.

claims.claim: The requirement of IGF signaling for Ihh expression seems to be restricted to a narrow perinatal window.
claims.source: Notably, the requirement of IGF signaling for Ihh expression seems to be restricted to a narrow perinatal window, as Igf1r deletion in the cartilage only reduces Ihh expression when triggered at P5 but not prenatally (Wang et al., 2011), and we show that Igf1 is no longer expressed in the IPFP by P12.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011 and the experimental data showing Igf1 expression dynamics.

claims.claim: Igf1r deletion in the cartilage only reduces Ihh expression when triggered at P5 but not prenatally.
claims.source: Notably, the requirement of IGF signaling for Ihh expression seems to be restricted to a narrow perinatal window, as Igf1r deletion in the cartilage only reduces Ihh expression when triggered at P5 but not prenatally (Wang et al., 2011), and we show that Igf1 is no longer expressed in the IPFP by P12.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claims.claim: mTORC1 was induced in the left pAC and RZ of P1-Pit::DTR mice despite reduction of local IGF1 levels.
claims.source: Unlike in the pre-HZ, we found mTORC1 activity was increased in the left pAC and RZ of P1-Pit::DTR mice. Since mTORC1 was induced despite reduction of local IGF1 levels, it follows that another signal must be responsible for mTORC1 activation in the AC/RZ.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing increased p-S6 in the pAC and RZ despite reduced Igf1.

claims.claim: IL6 expressed ectopically in the AC is a candidate signal responsible for mTORC1 activation in the AC/RZ, as this cytokine can activate mTORC1 in some cell types.
claims.source: One candidate is IL6 expressed ectopically in the AC, as this cytokine can activate mTORC1 in some cell types (Kim et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 activity dampened LEF1 levels in the RZ without impairing STAT3 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Interestingly, inhibition of mTORC1 activity dampened LEF1 levels in the RZ without impairing STAT3 phosphorylation, (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A'', C''), while JAK1/2 inhibition also precluded LEF1 upregulation, without impeding p-S6 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A',C').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A'', C''.

claims.claim: JAK1/2 inhibition precluded LEF1 upregulation, without impeding p-S6 activation.
claims.source: Interestingly, inhibition of mTORC1 activity dampened LEF1 levels in the RZ without impairing STAT3 phosphorylation, (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A'', C''), while JAK1/2 inhibition also precluded LEF1 upregulation, without impeding p-S6 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A',C').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A', C'.

claims.claim: Both mTORC1 and JAK/STAT signaling pathways are independently required to activate Lef1 expression.
claims.source: These results suggest that both mTORC1 and JAK/STAT signaling pathways are independently required to activate Lef1 expression (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and summarized in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The local influence exerted by the joint region could at least in part explain the fact that the proximal tibia and distal femur GPs grow faster than the distal tibia or proximal femur.
claims.source: We speculate that the local influence exerted by the joint region could at least in part explain poorly understood phenomena observed in the field of bone growth, such as the fact that the proximal tibia and distal femur GPs (i.e. closest to the fat pad) grow faster than the distal tibia or proximal femur (Digby, 1916; Payton, 1932; Moss-Salentijn, 1974).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings and citations to Digby, 1916; Payton, 1932; Moss-Salentijn, 1974.

claims.claim: Differential GP growth has been recently suggested to be evolutionary optimized to achieve energy-efficient scaling of the growing bones by minimizing the remodeling of ossified cortical structures.
claims.source: Our proposal is biologically relevant because differential GP growth has been recently suggested to be evolutionary optimized to achieve energy-efficient scaling of the growing bones by minimizing the remodeling of ossified cortical structures (Stern et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stern et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Classic experiments showed a change in growth rate upon proximo-distal transposition of the GPs within a bone, strongly suggesting the involvement of local extrinsic factors.
claims.source: While intrinsic differences in the GP likely exist and account in part for differential growth of proximal and distal GPs, classic experiments showed a change in growth rate upon proximo-distal transposition of the GPs within a bone (Moss-Salentijn, 1974; Hert, 1964), strongly suggesting the involvement of local extrinsic factors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moss-Salentijn, 1974; Hert, 1964.

claims.claim: Adipocyte-secreted signals can stimulate long bone growth in the absence of growth hormone.
claims.source: Fat pads are probably one of the main participants in this process, as suggested by our study and those of others showing that adipocyte-secreted signals can stimulate long bone growth in the absence of growth hormone (Shtaif et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shtaif et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The finding that Igf1 is almost absent from the IPFP by P8 correlates with the fact that the femur and tibia grow faster than the rest of the body (including forelimb bones) until roughly the same stage.
claims.source: In this regard, our finding that Igf1 is almost absent from the IPFP by P8 correlates with the fact that the femur and tibia grow faster than the rest of the body (including forelimb bones) until roughly the same stage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and [Roselló-Díez and Joyner, 2015]).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and citation to Roselló-Díez and Joyner, 2015.

claims.claim: The GP likely becomes independent from the IPFP after ~P8 due both to the intervening presence of the secondary ossification center as well as to cessation of Igf1 expression in the fat pad.
claims.source: The GP likely becomes independent from the IPFP after ~P8 (due both to the intervening presence of the secondary ossification center as well as to cessation of Igf1 expression in the fat pad), which could also explain why it takes longer for bone growth to be significantly impaired when the injury is induced at P14 vs. P1.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data comparing P1 and P14 injury models.

claims.claim: Local tissues hosting cells with osteochondrogenic potential, such as the synovium, bone marrow or the perichondrial groove of Ranvier, can contribute to bone growth not only with paracrine signals, but also with progenitor cells.
claims.source: Finally, we cannot exclude the possibility that the IPFP and/or other local tissues hosting cells with osteochondrogenic potential, such as the synovium, bone marrow or the perichondrial groove of Ranvier (Hindle et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013; Karlsson et al., 2009; Chung and Xian, 2014), can contribute to bone growth not only with paracrine signals, but also with progenitor cells (see for example Fig. S9 in [Yang et al., 2013]), such that cell death within these tissues in Pit::DTR mice depletes a pool of cells that participates in recovery of the injured bones.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on citations to Hindle et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013; Karlsson et al., 2009; Chung and Xian, 2014.

results.result: The Pit::DTR mouse model successfully induces left-specific cell death in hindlimb mesenchyme following DT injection at P1, while sparing the growth plate (GP) chondrocytes due to the avascular nature of the GP and limited DT diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 collectively establish the Pit::DTR model's specificity and the GP-sparing effect. DTR expression is confirmed in left limb mesenchyme (C2), DT injection causes left-specific cell death (C3), but the GP is protected (C4). The diffusion barrier explanation (C5) is supported by both literature citation and ex vivo culture data showing high DT concentrations can trigger GP cell death (C6), confirming chondrocytes can respond to DT when the barrier is overcome.

results.result: Left hindlimb bones show progressive growth reduction following P1 DT injection, with ~5% length difference at 3 dpi plateauing at ~11% by 9 weeks, while forelimbs remain unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 demonstrate the primary phenotype with quantitative bone length measurements at multiple timepoints (n=4-16 per group) and appropriate controls. The left-specific effect is confirmed by the lack of forelimb involvement (C9), which correlates with minimal DTR expression in forelimbs. Statistical analysis appears appropriate with clear sample sizes reported.

results.result: P1-Pit::DTR mice exhibit transient systemic growth reduction affecting both body weight and right limb bones, likely due to cardiac cell death, but right limb length normalizes by the end of the growth period while left limb defects persist.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 document a confounding systemic effect with supporting data (body weight, bone measurements, histology, gene expression). The cardiac involvement (C11) is supported by DTR expression and TUNEL data in heart tissue. Critically, C14 demonstrates that right limb normalization distinguishes the left-specific effect from systemic effects, strengthening the main conclusion. However, this systemic effect complicates interpretation of early timepoint data.

results.result: The left hindlimb growth defect in P1-Pit::DTR mice is characterized by reduced chondrocyte proliferation in the proliferative zone, decreased hypertrophic zone height, and delayed secondary ossification center formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 identify the cellular mechanisms underlying the growth defect with multiple complementary approaches: EdU incorporation (C15, n=4 control, 7 experimental), histological measurements (C16, n=4 per group), Col10a1 in situ hybridization (C16), and skeletal staining (C17, n=5). The data are internally consistent and appropriate statistical analyses are reported.

results.result: The growth defect is not caused by increased EGFR signaling in hypertrophic chondrocytes, ablation of perichondrial osteoprogenitors, or increased cell death at the osteochondral junction.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 systematically exclude alternative mechanisms through immunohistochemistry (C18, C19, C21) and a complementary genetic model (C20, Osx::DTR). The Osx::DTR experiment is particularly strong, showing that near-complete osteoprogenitor ablation reduces cortical thickness but not longitudinal growth, definitively ruling out this mechanism. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-8 per condition).

results.result: Ihh and Gli1 expression are reduced in the left GP at P3, while Pthlh expression is unchanged. SHP2 inhibition rescues Ihh expression but not bone growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 document altered Hedgehog signaling with in situ hybridization data (C22-C24, n=8-16 animals) and a pharmacological rescue experiment (C25). The SHP2 inhibitor result is important as it demonstrates Ihh reduction is reversible but insufficient alone to explain the growth defect, suggesting multiple parallel pathways are affected. However, the lack of bone growth rescue could also reflect incomplete pathway restoration or timing issues.

results.result: mTORC1 signaling (assessed by p-S6 levels) is reduced in the left proliferative zone and pre-hypertrophic zone from P3-P5, and this can be mimicked by rapamycin treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 establish reduced mTORC1 activity with immunohistochemistry across multiple timepoints (n=3-23 per timepoint). The rapamycin experiment (C27) confirms the specificity of the p-S6 readout for mTORC1 activity and demonstrates that mTORC1 inhibition alone can impair growth, supporting a causal role. The data are well-controlled and internally consistent.

results.result: FGF signaling is not increased in the left GP, though Fgfr3 is downregulated in the secondary ossification center region. MCP5 is not detected, but WNT target Lef1 is upregulated in the resting zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 survey multiple signaling pathways with appropriate molecular markers. The negative results (C28, C30) are important for ruling out alternative mechanisms. The Lef1 upregulation (C31, n=5 at P3, 4 at P4, 3 at P5) is consistently observed and may contribute to the phenotype based on cited literature linking LEF1 to impaired chondrocyte differentiation. The Fgfr3 downregulation (C29) correlates with delayed secondary ossification center formation.

results.result: Igf1 expression is specifically and dramatically downregulated in the left infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) at 2-3 dpi, recovering by 4 dpi, while expression in other tissues and expression of Igf2 and Igf1r remain largely unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 identify a highly specific molecular change with in situ hybridization data (C32, n=10/12 showing downregulation; C33, n=2 showing recovery). The spatial and temporal specificity is well-documented through examination of multiple tissues (C34, C35). This is a key finding linking the injury to a known growth-promoting factor. The transient nature of the change (recovery by 4 dpi) is notable given the persistent growth defect.

results.result: SOCS3 expression is not differentially expressed between left and right GPs at P2 or P3.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 rules out altered IGF signaling downstream components with immunohistochemistry (n=4 at P2, 3 at P3). This negative result is important for establishing that reduced IGF1 availability, rather than altered signaling machinery, is responsible for the observed effects. The sample size is adequate for this negative result.

results.result: Intraarticular IGF1 injection rescues mTORC1 signaling in the proliferative and pre-hypertrophic zones and also rescues Ihh and Fgfr3 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 demonstrate a causal relationship between IGF1 loss and signaling defects through a gain-of-function rescue experiment. The rescue of multiple pathways (mTORC1, Ihh, Fgfr3) by IGF1 alone (n=3-5 animals) suggests IGF1 is upstream of these pathways. This is strong evidence for the IPFP-GP signaling axis. However, the fact that IGF1 injection doesn't rescue bone growth (shown later) indicates additional mechanisms are involved.

results.result: Left-specific neutrophil and macrophage recruitment occurs in the IPFP at P2-P4, correlating temporally with Igf1 downregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 document inflammatory cell recruitment with immunohistochemistry across multiple timepoints (C39, n=5 per timepoint for neutrophils; C40 for macrophages). The temporal correlation between neutrophil infiltration and Igf1 downregulation is compelling. Quantification is provided for neutrophils (C39) with appropriate paired statistical analysis. The data support an inflammation-mediated mechanism for Igf1 suppression.

results.result: Neutrophil blockade with NIMP-R14 antibody partially restores Igf1 expression in the IPFP and increases p-S6 and Ihh levels in the pre-hypertrophic zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 establish a causal role for neutrophils in Igf1 suppression through antibody-mediated depletion. The partial rescue of Igf1 (C41, n=4) and downstream signaling (C42, n=3) demonstrates neutrophils contribute to but don't fully account for Igf1 downregulation. The experiment is well-controlled with verification of neutrophil depletion efficacy. This is strong mechanistic evidence linking inflammation to growth plate signaling defects.

results.result: LPS injection into WT mouse joints causes neutrophil recruitment and Igf1 downregulation in the absence of cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 provide independent validation that inflammation alone (without cell death) can suppress Igf1 expression. This LPS experiment is a strong control demonstrating the sufficiency of neutrophil recruitment for Igf1 suppression. The spatial correlation between neutrophil accumulation and Igf1 loss (C43) and the absence of cell death (C44) are well-documented with appropriate staining methods.

results.result: TNFα-expressing cells, including neutrophils, are present in the left IPFP at P2, and TNFα has been shown to reduce Igf1 expression in other tissues.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 identifies a candidate mediator of Igf1 suppression with immunohistochemistry showing TNFα in neutrophils. Claim C46 provides literature support for TNFα's ability to suppress Igf1. However, this remains correlative - no direct test of TNFα's role is performed. The intracellular localization of TNFα in neutrophils (Golgi-like) is interesting but the functional significance is unclear. This represents a plausible but unproven mechanism.

results.result: Neither IGF1 injection nor neutrophil blockade alone rescue bone growth at P4, and Lef1 expression remains elevated after both treatments.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 demonstrate that the IGF1/inflammation axis is necessary but not sufficient for normal growth. The failure of single interventions to rescue growth (C48, n=5 per treatment) despite rescuing multiple signaling pathways indicates parallel mechanisms. The persistent Lef1 upregulation (C49) after both treatments suggests an IGF1-independent pathway contributes to the phenotype. This is critical for establishing the two-pathway model presented later.

results.result: The immediate-early gene Egr1 is upregulated in the left IPFP and prospective articular cartilage at P2, with expression persisting in the articular cartilage through P4 before receding by P5.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 document activation of the injury response with in situ hybridization across multiple timepoints (n=2-3 per timepoint). The differential temporal dynamics between IPFP (transient) and articular cartilage (persistent) are well-characterized. Egr1 is an appropriate marker for the immediate-early injury response. The data establish that injury signaling is activated in the articular cartilage adjacent to the GP.

results.result: p-S6 expression is upregulated in the left prospective articular cartilage at P3-P4, receding by P5, suggesting transiently increased mTORC1 signaling in this region.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 documents increased mTORC1 activity in the articular cartilage (n=33 at P3, 14 at P4, 2 at P5) - opposite to the decrease observed in the pre-HZ. The citation to osteoarthritis literature (Pal et al., 2015) provides context for this finding. The large sample size at P3 strengthens confidence in this observation. This establishes distinct signaling responses in different regions of the joint.

results.result: Hif2a and Il6 are upregulated in the left prospective articular cartilage, leading to ectopic JAK1/2-dependent p-STAT3 expression at P3-P4 that recedes by P5.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 establish a signaling cascade in the injured articular cartilage with in situ hybridization (C53-C54) and immunohistochemistry (C55, n=13 at P3, 3 at P4). The citations linking Hif2a and Il6 to cartilage pathology provide mechanistic context. The temporal dynamics are well-characterized. The JAK1/2 dependence is later confirmed pharmacologically. This pathway is distinct from the IPFP-mediated effects.

results.result: The injury response in the prospective articular cartilage (Egr1, p-S6, p-STAT3) is independent of IPFP inflammation, as it persists after neutrophil blockade or IGF1 injection.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 establishes the independence of the two pathways (IPFP inflammation vs. articular cartilage injury response) through intervention experiments. This is critical for the two-pathway model. The data demonstrate that preventing IPFP inflammation doesn't block articular cartilage injury signaling, indicating these are parallel rather than sequential pathways. Sample sizes are not explicitly stated but the conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: Extensive and persistent cell loss occurs in the prospective/articular cartilage from P4 to at least P27, with signaling changes extending beyond the area of cell death into the resting zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 document the extent and persistence of articular cartilage damage with histology (n=3-4 animals). The observation that signaling changes extend beyond the area of cell death (C58) is important for establishing paracrine effects on the adjacent resting zone. The long-term persistence (P27) of the damage is notable and suggests permanent structural changes to the joint.

results.result: Cells in the prospective/articular cartilage do not normally give rise to growth plate chondrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by citation to lineage tracing work (Kozhemyakina et al., 2015). This is important for establishing that the articular cartilage effects on the GP must be paracrine rather than through altered cell contribution. The claim relies entirely on cited literature, which is appropriate for this type of background information.

results.result: JAK1/2 inhibition with ruxolitinib prevents p-STAT3 and LEF1 upregulation in the articular region but fails to rescue bone growth, possibly because mTORC1 signaling remains downregulated in the pre-hypertrophic zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 test the articular cartilage pathway with pharmacological inhibition. The successful blockade of p-STAT3 and LEF1 (C60) confirms JAK1/2 dependence. The failure to rescue growth (C61, n=5) despite blocking this pathway parallels the IGF1 injection results, supporting the two-pathway model. The explanation for failure (persistent mTORC1 downregulation) is plausible but somewhat speculative - other mechanisms could also explain the lack of rescue.

results.result: Combined treatment with ruxolitinib and IGF1 significantly rescues bone growth, though only some femora (3/11) and no tibiae show complete rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 provide the key test of the two-pathway model. The significant rescue with combined treatment (n=11) but not single treatments demonstrates that both pathways contribute to the growth defect. However, the incomplete rescue (C63) indicates additional mechanisms may be involved or that the interventions are not fully effective. The differential response between femora and tibiae (C63) is interesting but unexplained. Statistical analysis appears appropriate.

results.result: DT injection at P14 (P14-Pit::DTR model) causes cell death in surrounding soft tissues but not the GP, reduces hypertrophic zone height at 4 dpi, and leads to progressive left-right asymmetry (~7-13% by P57) that is non-significant at P20.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 establish that the injury model works at a later developmental stage but with different kinetics. The GP-sparing effect persists (C64, n=4), the cellular phenotype is similar (C65, n=2), but the growth defect develops more slowly (C66, n=3-7 per timepoint). The non-significance at P20 followed by significance at P57 suggests a cumulative effect. Sample sizes are smaller than the P1 model, particularly at P20 (n=3-4).

results.result: In P14-Pit::DTR mice, mTORC1 activity and Ihh signaling are not reduced in the left hypertrophic zone at 3-4 dpi, and Igf1 is no longer expressed in either IPFP by P17-18.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 demonstrate stage-specific differences in the mechanism. The absence of mTORC1/Ihh reduction (C67, n=4) and the lack of IPFP Igf1 expression (C68, n=3) indicate the IPFP-HZ axis is not active at P14. This is consistent with the developmental analysis showing Igf1 expression declines postnatally. The data support the conclusion that the GP becomes independent of IPFP-derived IGF1 after the secondary ossification center forms.

results.result: Egr1 and LEF1 are ectopically activated in the left cartilage of P14-Pit::DTR mice, similar to P1-Pit::DTR mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 shows the articular cartilage injury response pathway remains active at P14 (n=4). This indicates that while the IPFP-HZ axis is stage-specific, the articular cartilage-RZ axis persists. This helps explain why P14 injury still causes growth defects, albeit with slower kinetics. The data are consistent with the two-pathway model.

results.result: The IPFP appears as a defined region at E17.5, coinciding with accumulation of high Igf1 expression compared to surrounding tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 characterize the developmental emergence of the IPFP and its Igf1 expression. The data establish when this tissue becomes a potential source of IGF1 for the adjacent GP. The histological and in situ hybridization data are appropriate for this descriptive analysis. This provides important developmental context for understanding the stage-specific effects observed in the injury models.

results.result: Perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) are present in the interzone before IPFP formation, but adipocytes are not clearly visible until P3-P4, indicating adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 identify the cellular source of Igf1 in the IPFP through immunohistochemistry for cell type markers (n≥2 per stage). The temporal dissociation between Igf1 expression (high from E17.5) and adipocyte appearance (P3-P4) argues against adipocytes as the primary source. The perivascular stem cells are a plausible alternative source. The conclusion is logical but somewhat indirect - direct demonstration of which cells express Igf1 would be stronger.

results.result: Igf1 expression in the IPFP gradually decreases postnatally, becoming barely detectable at P8 and undetectable at P12.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 documents the temporal dynamics of Igf1 expression with in situ hybridization across multiple stages (n≥2 per stage). This is critical for explaining why the P14 injury model doesn't show IPFP-mediated effects. The gradual decline and eventual loss of expression is well-documented and consistent with the functional data from the injury models.

results.result: The radius grows more slowly than the tibia when Igf1 levels are high in the IPFP, with the ratio stabilizing after P8 when Igf1 expression ceases.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 provides correlative evidence that IPFP-derived Igf1 may contribute to differential bone growth under normal conditions. The radius/tibia ratio measurements (n≥4 per stage) show appropriate statistical analysis. The correlation between ratio stabilization and Igf1 cessation is intriguing but remains correlative. The radius lacks an adjacent fat pad, making it a reasonable control, but other factors could also explain differential growth rates.

results.result: The study demonstrates that transient mesenchymal cell death surrounding postnatal growth plates leads to reduced bone growth through altered paracrine signaling from two joint tissues: the IPFP and the prospective/articular cartilage.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C79, C80 represent the main conclusions of the study. The evidence from the entire manuscript supports a model where injury outside the GP affects growth through two parallel paracrine pathways. The IPFP pathway (inflammation→Igf1 loss→reduced mTORC1/Ihh in pre-HZ) and the articular cartilage pathway (injury response→IL6/STAT3/LEF1 in RZ) are both well-documented. The requirement for combined intervention to achieve rescue (C62) provides strong support for this two-pathway model.

results.result: Prior studies have shown that TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy and FGFs from the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 summarize relevant prior work through appropriate citations (Longobardi et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016). These claims provide context for the current study's contribution to understanding extrinsic regulation of bone growth. The citations appear accurate based on the descriptions provided.

results.result: The differential rescue of femora versus tibiae may reflect bone-specific differences in developmental stage-dependent responses to growth-modulating cues, as observed in other species with limb immobilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 offer a speculative explanation for the incomplete rescue observed in C63. While the citation to Pollard et al., 2017 (C82) provides precedent for bone-specific and stage-specific responses, the explanation remains speculative. Alternative explanations (e.g., incomplete drug penetration, dosing issues, additional unidentified pathways) are not excluded. The reasoning is plausible but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: Prior in vitro studies have shown that pro-inflammatory cytokines can impair bone growth beyond the cytokine exposure period, with only partial rescue by IGF1 treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 cite relevant prior work (MacRae et al., 2006; Mårtensson et al., 2004) that parallels the current findings. The citations provide context for the persistent growth defect despite transient inflammation and the incomplete rescue by IGF1 alone. The cited work appears accurately represented and relevant to the discussion.

results.result: Loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-hypertrophic zone correlates with loss of Ihh expression, both are rescued by IGF1, but IGF1 likely activates Ihh via an mTORC1-independent pathway, possibly through SHP2 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 dissect the relationship between IGF1, mTORC1, and Ihh through multiple complementary experiments: correlation (C85), IGF1 rescue (C86), SHP2 inhibition (C87), rapamycin treatment (C88-C89), leading to a mechanistic model (C90). The data support parallel rather than linear pathways downstream of IGF1. However, C90 is explicitly speculative ('we speculate') and the SHP2 mechanism is not directly tested. The model is plausible and consistent with the data but remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: The requirement for IGF signaling in Ihh expression appears restricted to a narrow perinatal window, as Igf1r deletion reduces Ihh only when triggered at P5 but not prenatally, and Igf1 expression in the IPFP ceases by P12.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 integrate cited literature (Wang et al., 2011) with the current study's developmental data to define a temporal window for IGF-Ihh regulation. The combination of published genetic data (C92) and the current expression analysis (C91) provides strong support for stage-specific regulation. This helps explain the differential effects of P1 versus P14 injury.

results.result: mTORC1 is activated in the left prospective articular cartilage and resting zone despite reduced local IGF1 levels, with IL6 as a candidate activating signal.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 documents the paradoxical mTORC1 activation (increased p-S6) in the articular cartilage/RZ despite reduced IGF1, based on the experimental data. Claim C94 proposes IL6 as a candidate mechanism with citation support (Kim et al., 2008). However, C94 is explicitly speculative and IL6's role in mTORC1 activation is not directly tested in this system. The observation is solid but the mechanism remains uncertain.

results.result: Both mTORC1 and JAK/STAT signaling pathways are independently required to activate Lef1 expression, as inhibition of either pathway prevents LEF1 upregulation without affecting the other pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 establish the relationship between mTORC1, JAK/STAT, and LEF1 through pharmacological inhibition experiments. The data show that rapamycin blocks LEF1 without affecting p-STAT3 (C95) and ruxolitinib blocks LEF1 without affecting p-S6 (C96), supporting independent requirement (C97). This is strong evidence for convergent regulation. Sample sizes are not explicitly stated but the conclusion is well-supported by the data shown.

results.result: Local joint influences could explain differential growth plate growth rates, as proximal tibia and distal femur (near the fat pad) grow faster than distal tibia or proximal femur, and classic transplantation experiments show growth rate changes with position.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 place the findings in a broader context of differential GP growth. The speculation (C98) is supported by multiple lines of evidence: classic transplantation experiments (C100), evolutionary optimization theory (C99), and adipocyte-derived growth signals (C101). All claims are appropriately supported by citations. However, C98 is explicitly speculative and the current study provides only indirect support through the IPFP-GP axis.

results.result: The cessation of Igf1 expression in the IPFP by P8 correlates with the stage when femur and tibia stop growing faster than the rest of the body, and the GP likely becomes independent from the IPFP after P8 due to the secondary ossification center and loss of Igf1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 integrate the developmental expression data with growth kinetics and the P14 injury model results. The correlation between Igf1 loss and growth rate normalization (C102) is supported by data and citation. The explanation for GP independence (C103) is logical and consistent with all the data, though it remains somewhat inferential. The two proposed mechanisms (physical barrier of secondary ossification center and loss of Igf1) are both plausible.

results.result: Local tissues with osteochondrogenic potential (synovium, bone marrow, perichondrial groove of Ranvier) may contribute to bone growth through both paracrine signals and progenitor cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 raises an alternative or additional mechanism involving progenitor cell contribution. The claim is appropriately cautious ('we cannot exclude') and supported by relevant citations (Hindle et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013; Karlsson et al., 2009; Chung and Xian, 2014). However, this possibility is not tested in the current study. The claim is speculative but acknowledges uncertainty and could explain why rescue is incomplete.
